description: We bring strong UI/UX, React, and 3D web execution.
summary:
Is It a Meteor Shower? started with a number that didn’t add up. In NASA’s Meteorite Landings data, recorded finds jump from 136 in the 1900s to 9,061 in the 2000s. That’s 66.6 times more. So are more meteors actually falling, or did we just get better at counting them?

It’s not just a trivia question. In February 2013, a meteor exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and injured more than 1,500 people. But the deeper we went into the dataset, the weirder it got. 6,214 records point to latitude 0, longitude 0, a spot in the Atlantic Ocean people call Null Island. No meteorites landed there. Those are records with missing coordinates.

So we cleaned the data first. Of the original 45,716 records, 31,911 were usable. We put 511 landings on an interactive Treasure Map, 19 of them in Indonesia. We also built Drop-a-Meteor, a simulator where you choose a meteor and see how much energy it releases, how big the crater would be, and how far the blast would reach.

To test the surge, we trained a Random Forest model, which reached 98.61% accuracy. Its answer: the sky isn’t getting busier. We’re just finding and recording more meteorites than we used to.

What came out of all this is a scrolling documentary, a map, and a simulator. You don’t need a science background to explore any of them.
details:
Is It a Meteor Shower? is a static website made with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and it’s hosted on Vercel. It has three pages. The scrolling documentary uses GSAP ScrollTrigger and Lenis for the scroll effects. The Treasure Map runs on Leaflet. The third page is Drop-a-Meteor, our impact simulator. All the charts are made with Chart.js.

The data work happens in Python Jupyter notebooks with pandas and scikit-learn. We started with 45,716 records from NASA’s Meteorite Landings dataset and cleaned them down to 31,911. Then we used K-Means to group the landing sites into five geographic zones. To check whether the jump in finds is real, we trained a Random Forest classifier. It scored 98.61% accuracy with a ROC-AUC of 0.9946.

We also pulled in data from a few other sources: 888 bolides from NASA CNEOS fireballs, JPL’s Sentry and Close Approach Data, the NeoWs feed, and SEDAC’s GPWv4 population grid.

All of our code is open source on GitHub (https://github.com/saaandbite/spaceapp). Every number on the site is calculated straight from the raw data, so you can check any of it yourself.
